text:
Kai: Morning team! First-day bootstrap question. Using an M2 Mac and also set up WSL2 on a Windows laptop for parity. My dotfiles try to keep `asdf/.tool-versions` in sync, but builds differ: on mac `asdf install ruby 3.1.4` pulls in openssl and works, on WSL ruby build fails with `checking for readline/readline.h... no`. Also my zsh on mac doesn't pick up asdf shims when VS Code opens via spotlight. Anyone got a neat cross-OS checklist?

Tess: Welcome Kai! :wave: Two quick notes: 1) On Linux you usually need `libreadline-dev` (and other -dev packages). On Ubuntu: `sudo apt install build-essential libssl-dev zlib1g-dev libreadline-dev libsqlite3-dev`. 2) For VS Code on mac, Spotlight opens a non-login shell; put asdf path/init in `.zshenv` so all shells see it.

Kai: Thanks — installed the apt packages and ruby build moved forward but then `mkmf.rb couldn't find header for openssl`. I have `openssl@3` on mac but WSL has `libssl-dev` installed. Strange mismatch.

Jakob: On mac brew installs are keg-only; you often need to point build flags at `openssl@1.1` libs: `brew install openssl@1.1` then `export LDFLAGS="-L/opt/homebrew/opt/openssl@1.1/lib"` etc. On WSL, `libssl-dev` corresponds to system libs. If you want parity, prefer building both against openssl@1.1 or use asdf to pin a binary-friendly runtime.

Kai: Ok did the flags on mac and reinstalled ruby. Now pip for python installed via asdf is missing `wheel` at runtime and some C-extensions for a package fail to compile. I worry my `PATH` ordering or homebrew vs nix is confusing things. I do have Nix on the mac for experiments.

Tess: Nix can definitely inject headers/paths. For reproducible dev, one trick: create a temporary clean shell for asdf builds: `env -i PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/bin:/bin" LDFLAGS="$LDFLAGS" CPPFLAGS="$CPPFLAGS" asdf install python 3.11.4`. That avoids Nix shadows. After a successful build, normal shells can use the runtime.

Kai: That clean env trick fixed python. Next: my dotfiles use direnv to load secrets from 1Password via `eval "$(op signin)"` — but in GUI apps like VS Code I get `direnv: error: not allowed`. I assume it's because direnv needs `direnv allow` per repo?

Jakob: Right — direnv requires `direnv allow` for each `.envrc` change. GUI apps opening projects won't automatically run that. Best practice: keep `.envrc` minimal and have it source a `.envrc.local` that's gitignored; run `direnv allow` in a terminal once. For 1Password, ensure the CLI is logged in and `OP_SESSION` env var present in the shell. GUI apps launched from the dock won't inherit your terminal env unless you launch them from the terminal.

Kai: Makes sense. I launched VS Code from launcher earlier. Launching from terminal made direnv work. Last blocker: git pushes to our enterprise remote fail with `Permission denied (publickey)`. I can ssh to github fine but pushing to `git.redwood.ai` fails. Which team owns that?

infra-bot: Pinged platform-ssh: the enterprise git hosts use a jump-host key policy. If you see `Permission denied`, ensure your `~/.ssh/config` has `Host git.redwood.ai \n  HostName git.redwood.internal \n  User git \n  ProxyJump bastion.redwood.ai` and that your key is loaded with `ssh-add -l`. If using 1Password SSH agent, ensure `eval "$(op signin)"` and `op ssh sign-in` completed.

Tess: Also check `ssh -vT git@git.redwood.ai` for clues. If your key is present in 1Password but not attached to your account at the git host, open a ticket with `@platform` to add it.

Kai: Ran `ssh -vT`, saw the client trying `id_ed25519` but server rejecting. I loaded the correct key via `ssh-add ~/.ssh/redwood_id_ed25519` and push succeeded. Whew.

Kai: One small ergonomic ask: my dotfiles have `sync-dotfiles.sh` which rsyncs config between machines, but it clobbers the mac's `/opt/homebrew` PATH order; any recommended approach to keep machine-specific installs separate?

Jakob: We keep machine-specific overrides in `dotfiles/machines/<hostname>.env` and have the sync script skip brew-managed paths. Another pattern: commit `SETUP.md` with per-platform notes and include `dotfiles/.local` which is gitignored. When sync runs, it sources `.local` and doesn't overwrite system-managed files. Encourage a `PR` for the onboarding dotfiles with a `MACHINE.md` note.

Kai: Good idea — I'll add `machines/m1-pro.local` and a `SETUP.md` with brew/asdf notes. Final Q: any quick checklist I should follow so future hires don't hit the same traps?

Devex Bot: Welcome! Short checklist recommended for cross-OS parity: 1) commit `asdf/.tool-versions` in dotfiles, 2) add per-host `machines/<name>.local` gitignored, 3) on mac install `openssl@1.1 readline` and export build flags for asdf builds, 4) on WSL install distro `-dev` packages and prefer cloning into WSL filesystem, 5) put asdf init in `.zshenv` for mac, 6) run `direnv allow` in a terminal and launch GUI tools from terminal when testing envs, 7) ensure SSH keys loaded (ssh-add or 1Password) and `~/.ssh/config` has corporate ProxyJump if needed, 8) avoid committing secrets; use direnv + 1Password. Docs: https://redwood.ai/devex/bootstrap and open PRs to `github.com/redwood-onboarding/dotfiles` for reviews. Enjoy your first week! :tada:
